{{Short description|Elliptic curve associated with a Fermat triple}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Frey curve''' or '''Frey&ndash;Hellegouarch''' curve is the [[elliptic curve]] 
<math display="block"> y^2 = x(x - \alpha)(x + \beta)</math>
associated with an ABC triple <math> \alpha+\beta=\gamma </math>. This relates properties of solutions of equations to elliptic curves. This curve was popularized in its application to [[Fermat’s Last Theorem]] where one investigates a (hypothetical) solution of [[Fermat's Last Theorem|Fermat's equation]]
:<math>a^\ell + b^\ell = c^\ell.</math>
The curve is named after [[Gerhard Frey (mathematician)|Gerhard Frey]] and (sometimes) {{ill|Yves Hellegouarch|fr||de}}.

==History==
{{harvs|first=Yves|last=Hellegouarch|year=1975|txt}} came up with the idea of associating solutions <math>(a,b,c)</math> of Fermat's equation with a completely different mathematical object: an elliptic curve.{{sfnp|Hellegouarch|1975}} If ℓ is an [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] [[prime number|prime]] and ''a'', ''b'', and ''c'' are positive [[integer]]s such that
<math display="block">a^\ell + b^\ell = c^\ell, </math>
then a corresponding Frey curve is an algebraic curve given by the equation
<math display="block"> y^2 = x(x - a^\ell)(x + b^\ell), </math>
or, equivalently
<math display="block"> y^2 = x(x - a^\ell)(x - c^\ell).</math>
This is a nonsingular algebraic curve of [[Genus of an algebraic curve|genus]] one defined over '''Q''', and its [[Projectivization|projective completion]] is an elliptic curve over '''Q'''.

{{harvs|first=Gerhard|last=Frey|authorlink=Gerhard Frey (mathematician)|year=1982|txt}} called attention to the unusual properties of the same curve as Hellegouarch, which became called a Frey curve. This provided a bridge between Fermat and Taniyama by showing that a [[counterexample]] to Fermat's Last Theorem would create such a curve that would not be modular. The conjecture attracted considerable interest when {{harvtxt|Frey|1986}} suggested that the [[Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture]] implies Fermat's Last Theorem.{{sfnmp|1a1=Frey|1y=1982|2a1=Frey|2y=1986}} However, his argument was not complete. In 1985, [[Jean-Pierre Serre]] proposed that a Frey curve could not be modular and provided a partial proof of this. This showed that a proof of the semistable case of the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture would imply Fermat's Last Theorem. Serre did not provide a complete proof and what was missing became known as the [[epsilon conjecture]] or ε-conjecture. In the summer of 1986, {{harvtxt|Ribet|1990}} proved the epsilon conjecture, thereby proving that the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture implies Fermat's Last Theorem.{{sfnp|Ribet|1990}}
